title: Pandora and the box
subtitle: The jar of evils
subject: mythologie
description: The first woman created by the gods, Pandora opens a jar full of plagues. Deep down there remains hope. A myth about curiosity and misfortune.

hero.hook: It wasn't a box. It was a jar. And what it contained changed the fate of humans.

blocks.text: In Greek mythology, **Pandora** is not just a character. She is the first woman, shaped by the gods as a trap. **Zeus** wants to punish the men who were shot by [[Prometheus]].

Pandora arrives with a jar. By opening it, she releases the evils that put an end to human carelessness. Deep down there remains an enigmatic thing: the **hope**. This is how the expression “opening Pandora’s box” is born.

After the theft of fire, Zeus orders **Hephaestus**, god of forging, to model a woman in clay and water, beautiful as a goddess. Each Olympian adds a donation. **Athena** teaches him weaving. **Aphrodite** gives it the charm. **Hermes**, messenger of the gods, tricks and lies into him.

blocks.caption: Pandora, “she who received all gifts”, created to deceive men.

blocks.text: She is called **Pandora**: “the one who received all the gifts”. Prometheus had warned his brother **Epimetheus** not to accept any gifts from Zeus. Too late. Epimetheus, the one who thinks afterwards, falls under the spell and welcomes it.
Among the Greeks, Pandora was not created as a companion. It is designed as a punishment, a “beautiful evil” intended to strike humanity.

sections.title: The jar opens, the plagues fly away

blocks.text: Pandora carries a “pithos”, a large storage jar. Latin texts and modern translations will make it a “box”. Inside, the gods locked away old age, disease, famine, madness, war.
The “box” error comes from [[Erasmus of Rotterdam]], in the 16th century. When translating Hesiod, he confuses “pithos” (jar) and “pyxis” (small box).

Driven by the curiosity that the gods have placed in her, Pandora lifts the lid. The plagues escape at once. Panicked, she closes the jar. Too late. Only [[Elpis (Hope)]], Hope, remains, clinging to the bottom.
Why does hope remain in the jar? Since Antiquity, there has been debate. If the container only contained evils, are we to believe that hope is one?
For some, like the philosopher **Nietzsche**, hope prolongs the torment: it prevents us from accepting reality. For others, Zeus left it on purpose, as the only remedy for despair.
In Greek, [[Elpis (Hope)]] is not only positive. The word refers to the expectation of what is to come, good or bad. A neutral force, capable of saving or tormenting.

In **Hesiod**, author of the Theogony, the story of Pandora carries a strong [[Misogyny]]: the woman appears there as a burden for the man. This myth has often been compared to Eve and the biblical fall.
In other versions, the jar contained benefits. By flying towards Olympus, they would have become inaccessible to mortals.

Later, Pandora also becomes the figure of curiosity. His disobedience brings misfortune, but also pushes humanity to work, invent, survive. Today, “opening Pandora’s box” refers to an action with uncontrollable consequences.
The **Pandora** jar puts an end to human carelessness. Evils spread, and **hope** remains at the bottom: the only counterpoint, ambiguous, in the face of misfortune.
